selected.name: Global closure of local alternatives
selected.instruction: Score 10 when pointwise possibilities are shown to combine into one globally consistent form, with mixed assignments explicitly ruled out; score 0 when the post stops after listing possibilities for each individual input.
selected.rationale: Rows R16 and R25 first obtain the pointwise alternatives 0, x^2, and -x^2, then address the essential mixed-pattern obstruction. This is evidence of solving the global problem rather than only deriving local constraints.

selected.name: Explicit claim-proof structuring
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the solution contains multiple explicitly labeled claims or lemmas (using 'Claim:', 'Lemma:', or equivalent markers), each with its own proof block. Score 0 if the solution is unstructured flowing prose or raw calculations with no organizational markers.
selected.rationale: R07, R45, R49, R57, R60 (dense_high) use labeled claim-proof structure. R03, R18, R29 (dense_low) lack such structure. The scorecard may not weight this organizational hallmark heavily enough.
member_names: Density of formal Claim / Lemma / Proof scaffolding
Intermediate results promoted to stated, proved claims

selected.name: Isolable pivotal-fact statement
selected.instruction: Score whether the post states a single crisp pivotal identity, lemma, or structural fact as a self-contained claim that could stand alone as the crux of a solution, independent of whether surrounding derivation or final computation is completed. A 10: a specific formula/identity/lemma is explicitly isolated and named as the key fact (e.g., stated on its own line or flagged as 'the key point is...'), even if little else is derived. A 0: no such isolable pivotal fact ever appears; the post is either a diffuse mass of computation with no single fact singled out, or contains no mathematical content at all.
selected.rationale: R52 states only the monovariant idea ('the difference between the largest and smallest a_i') without any write-up, and R59 states only the identity F_2n/F_n = F_{n+1}+F_{n-1} without deriving it or finishing the computation; both are terse to the point of being unfinished, yet both carry dense_pct far above card_pct, suggesting the dense model credits a correctly isolated crux fact even when nothing else is shown.
member_names: Names the pivotal idea in plain words
Pivotal idea named in standard terms, execution aside

selected.name: Single external theorem does all the work
selected.instruction: Score how much of the argument is discharged by invoking one heavy named or external result whose statement is not proved or unpacked in the post. 10 = no such invocation; every step is carried out on the objects of the problem. 0 = essentially the whole problem is dispatched by one citation - the hook-length formula for Young tableaux (with a link), Minkowski's inequality applied once to get the answer, a scaling trick that manufactures the answer in two lines - so that the post contains almost no reasoning specific to this problem. Mid scores when a named result is invoked but substantial problem-specific work surrounds it.
selected.rationale: R29 (dense 0.254, card 0.953) is a single hook-length citation with an external URL; R32 (dense 0.268, card 0.901) is one application of Minkowski; R33 (dense 0.108, card 0.729) is a one-shot scaling construction. All three are near the top of the scorecard and near the bottom of the dense ranking, so a rubric that credits correctness and concision will over-reward exactly this shape.
member_names: Named theorem as embedded step vs. sole content
One cited heavyweight theorem does all the work
Single external theorem does all the work

selected.name: Names and separately addresses a trap or edge case
selected.instruction: Score whether the post explicitly names a specific trap, degenerate configuration, or edge case (rather than only implicitly handling it inside general casework) and pauses to address it as its own labeled step. A 10: a specific trap/edge case is explicitly named (e.g., 'the pointwise trap', 'if a=b this fails', 'the degenerate case where...') and separately resolved. A 0: no edge case or trap is ever explicitly named as such, even if some casework is present.
selected.rationale: R24 has a section explicitly headed 'We now deal with the pointwise trap' with three enumerated subcases; R31 structures its final claims (Claims 2-4) explicitly around ruling out specific degenerate value-pairings the pointwise ambiguity could produce. Both carry high dense_pct (0.921 and 0.817) with low card_pct.
member_names: Degenerate or pitfall branch identified and killed
Names and closes the known failure mode of its own route
Names and separately addresses a trap or edge case

selected.name: Absence of unconventional-approach markers
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the post contains NO language self-labeling the approach as unusual, unconventional, or excessive (e.g., 'troll,' 'scuffed,' 'overkill,' 'different,' 'cheap,' 'ridiculous'). Score 0 if multiple such markers appear, signaling the author themselves recognizes the approach deviates from standard.
selected.rationale: R05 ('Scuffed troll solution'), R28 ('ridiculous and yet ultimately equivalent...overkill'), R10 ('different from the others'), R25 ('very cheap but fast'), and R30 ('for those who understand less') all self-label as non-standard and are dense_low. Dense-high items like R01, R43, R34 contain no such markers. The author's own awareness of non-canonical approach is a strong signal the dense model detects.
member_names: Advertises itself as a departure from the usual treatment
Post self-brands its route as a deviation or a stunt

selected.name: Post questions or disowns the argument it posts
selected.instruction: Score the post's stance toward the reasoning it displays. 10: the post asserts its argument as correct and finished. 5: the post asserts the argument but hedges about a specific step. 0: the post displays reasoning it does not stand behind -- asks why its answer is wrong, asks whether the approach works, or reproduces someone else's argument in order to object to it.
selected.rationale: R07 lays out a full derivation, reaches 391, and closes with 'Can someone please explain why 391 is incorrect?'; R58 reproduces a wiki argument and asks 'Wouldn't that be overcounting?'; R34 presents a two-case proof under the heading 'Does this work?'. A criterion bank scoring the mathematics on the page will read all three as substantial and largely well-formed, since the displayed work is long and structured, and will have no slot for the author's own repudiation of it.
member_names: Asserts a solution versus queries or corrects one
Post questions or disowns the argument it posts

selected.name: Generalizes beyond the minimum needed
selected.instruction: Score whether the post goes beyond exactly what is needed to answer the stated problem, e.g. by extending the argument to a broader family (different n, different configuration), stating additional properties of the configuration, or adding a labeled 'further observations' section. A 10: the post clearly extends its reasoning or findings beyond the minimal answer, with the extension clearly marked as bonus/general material. A 0: the post stops the instant the requested quantity is obtained, with no exploration of the broader structure.
selected.rationale: R20 solves the specific 10-move triangle question quickly, then extends its method to general n-gon random walks and takes a limit as k→∞; R48 answers the requested AB^2 and then adds an 'Other Observations' section on the K-symmedian and the P-Dumpty point. Both carry high dense_pct (0.865, 0.762) despite low card_pct.
member_names: Engages structure beyond the question asked
Explores the configuration beyond the minimum needed

selected.name: Algebraic step transparency
selected.instruction: Score 10 if all key algebraic manipulations are shown step by step with no major leaps. Score 0 if the post jumps directly to results with significant intermediate algebra omitted.
selected.rationale: R03 shows detailed algebraic manipulation throughout its case analysis—dense-high. R19 condenses the entire Minkowski argument into one line with the factorization (S_n-n²)(S_n+n²)=1·289 appearing without derivation—dense_low. The scorecard credits the elegant one-liner; the dense model may see the omitted steps as a departure from the canonical derivation.

selected.name: Completeness of candidate classification
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the post both derives all possible candidates and directly verifies that each candidate satisfies the original conditions; score 0 when it guesses candidates, verifies only some, or never excludes alternatives.
selected.rationale: R02 and R42 classify and check all functional-equation solutions, whereas R28 and R25 give conclusions with little candidate analysis.

selected.name: Objective-preserving optimization
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the varying target is rigorously reduced to a simpler quantity using a fixed or monotone factor, and the optimization direction is preserved; score 0 when calculations are performed without establishing that they optimize the requested quantity.
selected.rationale: Row R23 reduces the area minimization to minimizing AX, while R45 reduces an integer condition to a sharp Minkowski bound. This captures whether the optimization target is structurally controlled.

selected.name: Method sophistication proportionality to problem
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the mathematical tools used are proportionate in sophistication to the apparent difficulty of the problem (e.g., elementary number theory for a modular arithmetic problem). Score 0 if the method is wildly over-powered (e.g., finite field theory for a root-of-unity computation) or under-powered for the problem.
selected.rationale: R28 uses F_25 finite field computation for a problem solvable by identifying an 8th root of unity—dense_low_card_high. R06 constructs elaborate perpendicular line verifications for a simple angle formula—dense_low. R43 uses Cauchy-Schwarz for an inequality where it is the natural tool—dense-high. The dense model appears to credit methods that match the problem's intended difficulty level.

selected.name: Exact modular periodicity
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the post proves a valid period or residue restriction and then uses it exhaustively to constrain the target; score 0 when it merely reports a pattern or invokes a modulus without justifying all relevant cases.
selected.rationale: R10 uses parity and modulo 3 cycles, R17 uses root-of-unity periodicity, and R40 combines congruences to exclude all larger cases.

selected.name: Strategic use of symmetry
selected.instruction: Score 10 when symmetry, invariance, or an interchangeable reformulation materially reduces the argument and is used correctly; score 0 when symmetry is absent, accidental, or merely mentioned without consequence.
selected.rationale: R23 exploits circular ordering and R40 exploits cyclic equality conditions, while R26 and R58 use geometric or algebraic observations without a sound symmetry-based reduction.

selected.name: Exploits the multiple-choice option list
selected.instruction: For posts on problems that display answer choices (A)-(E). 10 = the post determines the answer as a value, never using the option list except to report the letter at the end. 0 = the option list is load-bearing: the post computes a residue or parity and picks the unique surviving choice, or argues that the choices are far enough apart that a coarse computation distinguishes them, or works in a substitute setting on the grounds that the listed answers are distinguishable there. Score 5 if the option list is used only as a final sanity check on an independently obtained value. Score 5 for problems with no answer choices.
selected.rationale: R52 (dense 0.324, card 0.886) admits it is 'very cheap' and selects the only choice that is odd and 1 mod 3; R44 (dense 0.140, card 0.848) argues explicitly that 'the answer choices are all clearly distinct and extant over F_25' and then works there; R23 (dense 0.274, card 0.923) approximates its way to a neighbourhood of 72 and reads off a choice. All three are card-top and dense-low, so the scorecard is crediting a shortcut that does not answer the underlying question.
member_names: Computes the asked quantity rather than eliminating options

selected.name: Inter-post referencing and sequence markers
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the text explicitly references other posts, posters, or its place in the thread sequence. Look for phrases such as '@above', 'as above', 'previous post', 'Solution 2', 'different from the others', 'similar to what was posted', or direct replies to a named user. Do not judge whether referencing is good or bad; score only how much such referencing is present.
selected.rationale: Posts that engage earlier contributions leave conversational markers that make them non-standalone; this is independent of whether their mathematical method matches the canonical write-up. R12 says 'I already addressed this in my previous post'; R21 begins '@above'; R08 says 'similar to above'.
member_names: Back-reference language presupposing earlier posts in the thread
Backward reference to earlier thread activity

selected.name: Collaboration attribution
selected.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of explicit references to collaborators, helpers, prior assistance, or thanking another participant; do not judge the value of that assistance.
selected.rationale: Collaboration leaves visible attribution traces and may also influence which route the author adopts, making this mixed. Examples include R16, R34, and R53.
upstream_parent_all_members: author's social embedding on the forum (study group, mutuals, following) — an unseen factor whose only textual trace is the credit line
author's social network / collaborative solving culture

selected.name: Colloquial and emotional register
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text uses informal colloquial language, slang, self-deprecation, emoticons, or emotional interjections (e.g., 'rip', 'cuz', ':(', 'nooooo', 'Bro'), as opposed to standard mathematical prose. 0 = entirely formal; 10 = heavily colloquial/emotional. Do not judge whether informality is good or bad.
selected.rationale: R01 ('I assumed... didn't really know why... :(') and R22 ('Bro... cuz im dumb... RIP') are dense_high_card_low: the dense model may key on approach content while the scorecard is put off by register. R09 ('Dangit') and R25 ('Holy cow') show the same split.
selected.upstream_parent: poster's practice in the format / audience expectation
member_names: Casual affect, interjections and self-deprecating chatter
upstream_parent_all_members: poster's audience (chatting with peers vs writing for a permanent record)
poster's practice in the format / audience expectation
the poster's audience — peers reading in real time versus a stranger arriving later by search

selected.name: Markup scaffolding
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the post uses visual organization such as hides, colored headings, bullets, boxed answers, quote blocks, or elaborate sectioning; do not judge whether this feature is good.
selected.rationale: R04 uses colored claims, R23 uses multiple colored sections, and R29 uses hidden blocks and lemma headings. The amount of forum presentation scaffolding is a formatting nuisance independent of mathematical merit.
member_names: Forum markup furniture: hide blocks, colour-tagged claims, boxed answers
Rich forum markup and structured formatting
upstream_parent_all_members: author's practice and fluency in the forum format
the poster's habitual markup practice, itself a function of how long they have been posting in this format
typographic habit / poster's practice in the format

selected.name: Answer-choice anchoring
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the post foregrounds answer choices, option letters, boxed numerical outputs, or answer-checking language. Judge only this assessment-format trace; do not judge whether it is good.
selected.rationale: R12 explicitly corrects an answer choice, R33 identifies choice C, and R46 dismisses choice E. These visible test-taking conventions can affect reception without indicating the substantive solution approach.
member_names: Multiple-choice answer-extraction framing in the post
upstream_parent_all_members: the kind of problem the thread hangs off (short computational contest item versus open-ended olympiad problem), which sets the population of posters and their norms

selected.name: Contest-conditions self-report and score talk
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the post narrates the circumstances of its own production under exam conditions: phrases such as 'my solution during the contest', 'in-contest', 'I wrote this on the test', reported grades or points ('somehow got a 7/7', 'hoping it's not more than 1 point off', 'I sure do hope it is valid'), reported elapsed time ('it took ~1.3 hours'), or comparisons to other problems on the same paper ('meanwhile I thought #4 was far harder'). 0 = the post says nothing about when or under what conditions it was written; 10 = several such self-reports, and the framing of the whole post is 'here is what I did on the day'. Score only how much such self-report is present. You must NOT judge whether the claim is credible or whether writing under contest conditions makes the post better or worse.
selected.rationale: R26 hides its body under 'My solution during the contest (different from the others)'; R60 opens 'Here is my solution during the contest, with bit modifications'; R58 opens 'Here is my cursed solution which somehow got a 7/7'; R28 reports '~1.3 hours' and 'I sure do hope it is valid'; R49 worries 'I'm hoping its not more than 1 point off'. This is a timing fingerprint: it says when the text was produced, not what route it takes. Tagged mixed because a contestant writing on the day has not yet read anyone else's approach, which can genuinely shift which route appears.
selected.upstream_parent: timing of production/submission relative to the competition (a same-week contestant post versus a later archival write-up)
upstream_parent_all_members: timing of production (live contest attempt vs. later leisure engagement)
timing of production/submission relative to the competition (a same-week contestant post versus a later archival write-up)

selected.name: Validation-seeking and uncertain posture
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post is framed as a question, request for checking, or expression of doubt rather than a confident solution. Look for phrases like 'Does this work?', 'Can someone please explain why', 'Wouldn't that be overcounting?', or 'I'm getting X, is this right?'. Do not judge whether the uncertainty is warranted; score only how much the text seeks validation.
selected.rationale: A post can contain substantial mathematics yet be framed as an inquiry, which may inflate a checklist score without matching the canonical approach. R18 asks 'Does this work?'; R37 asks 'Can someone please explain why 391 is incorrect?'; R38 asks 'Wouldn't that be overcounting?'
member_names: Help-seeking and uncertainty posture toward one's own post
upstream_parent_all_members: the poster's standing and seniority on the forum, and their practice in this format

selected.name: Density of display mathematics and align environments
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 how much of this post's mathematics is set as centred display or in multi-line aligned environments rather than run inline inside sentences. Consider the proportion of equations that are broken out on their own lines, the use of aligned/align-star or eqnarray blocks, chains of implication set on separate display lines, and tabular blocks. 0 = all mathematics is inline within running prose; 10 = the post is essentially a stack of display blocks with connective text between them. Do NOT judge whether the typesetting is attractive, readable or appropriate, and do NOT judge whether the mathematics is right. Score only the extent of display-versus-inline setting.
selected.rationale: Typesetting habit tracks how much the author has written in this format before, not which route the argument takes. R05 and R45 set nearly every step in aligned blocks, and R57 does the same, while R08 and R27 present essentially identical kinds of reasoning entirely inline (R27 even in lowercase running prose). The two presentations of the same manipulations should not be distinguished by an approach-match target, so any predictive power here is nuisance. Tagged mixed because practised typesetters are also practised solvers.
selected.upstream_parent: the poster's practice and fluency with the forum's typesetting conventions
member_names: Density of display mathematics and align environments
upstream_parent_all_members: the poster's practice and fluency with the forum's typesetting conventions
typographic habit / poster's practice in the format

selected.name: Explicit self-assessment labels
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post labels its own solution with qualitative descriptors such as 'cheap', 'fast', 'overkill', 'scuffed', 'troll', 'cursed', 'different', 'alternative', or 'simple'. Do not judge whether the label is accurate; score only how many such self-assessment phrases appear.
selected.rationale: Self-labeling can bias a scorer independently of the actual mathematical approach. R09 calls itself 'very cheap but fast'; R40 says 'Scuffed troll solution'; R54 says 'cursed solution which somehow got a 7/7'; R04 calls itself 'a different solution'.
upstream_parent_all_members: position in the entry stream (the pressure on a later poster to advertise that they add something the thread lacks)

selected.name: Legacy autocorrupted LaTeX and era-marked forum markup
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post carries typographic markers of an older era of this forum's software, judged purely by their presence. Count: math macros of the form backslash-equal-brace-brace and backslash-minus-brace-brace appearing where a plain equals sign or minus sign belongs; a stray space immediately after an opening dollar sign (for example a dollar sign followed by space then a numeral); bracketed url tags with a full http address inside the prose; double-square-bracket wiki-style links or File inclusions; hide tags whose argument is wrapped in double quotes rather than bare; and other markup that is not the modern plain form. 0 = none of these appear; 10 = they appear throughout. Do NOT judge whether old or new markup is better, cleaner or more readable, and do NOT judge the mathematics. Score only how much era-marked markup is visibly present.
selected.rationale: Pure dating artifact with zero bearing on which solution route is taken. R01 contains both the corrupted equals macro and a bracketed http url tag; R14 contains the corrupted minus and equals macros; R12 and R35 show the spaced-dollar-sign habit of the same period. A text-only model can read the decade off these tokens, so they are a live nuisance channel; nothing about them says anything about approach.
selected.upstream_parent: the calendar era in which the post was written (and later software migrations that rewrote old posts)
member_names: Era-marked markup, notation and link style
Legacy autocorrupted LaTeX and era-marked forum markup

the calendar era in which the post was written, i.e. how long after the thread opened it arrived
